items.article_search_text: Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton have opened up on the fallout from their costly Las Vegas crash. Read more at foxsports.com.au. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton have opened up on crunch talks after their Vegas crash, while Oscar Piastri is eyeing a big result at one of his best tracks. There was a time the Qatar Grand Prix seemed certain not to happen. Now organisers say it will be sold out. With Formula 1 unwilling to can the event despite rising tensions in the Persian Gulf, and with local organisers of both the Qatar race and next weekend’s event in Abu Dhabi insisting that circumstances are safe, the sport will conclude the 2026 season in the Middle East as planned. MotoGP, after all, has been there and done that, having held its Qatar Grand Prix safely earlier this month — and the two top-tier motorsport categories now share a parent company. Watch the final 2 qualifying sessions of the 2026 F1® season Live and Free with Kayo Freebies. Watch FORMULA 1 QATAR AIRWAYS QATAR GRAND PRIX 2026 qualifying session on Sunday 29th November > It means F1 will now get its run at one of its more extreme circuits. Replete with fast, demanding corners with few straight lines, this track is the definition of a tyre killer. It’s the only circuit on the calendar for which tyre supplier Pirelli mandates maximum stint lengths to prevent the tyres from reaching dangerous levels of structural wear. This year all tyre compounds are hard limited to 27 laps. In a 57-lap race, that means at least two stops per driver. The earliest the first stop can be made is at the end of lap 3. The latest is lap 27. If degradation is as low as it was last year, teams will be tempted to wait for a safety car. Last year every team except McLaren pitted during a lap 7 safety car that locked everyone into an identical strategy. Oscar Piastri, the pole-getter and leader, lost what could have been an easy victory. No-one will want to do a McLaren this season in the same circumstances. PIASTRI PREPARES FOR STRONG SEASON FINISH Piastri’s sensational 17th-to-third recovery drive at last weekend’s Las Vegas Grand Prix couldn’t have been better timed. In a season that’s offered few highlights, this weekend he has a chance to flex his muscles at by far his strongest circuit. He’s never finished a Qatar Grand Prix off the podium. His average finish is 2.3, the best result for any circuit in his career. His average grand prix score of 17 points per race (51 points in total) is by far the most of any venue. He’s outqualified Norris 2-1 at this track, and it’s one of eight circuits where he’s been faster on average over a single lap across all visits. He scored one of his six poles here too. If you include sprints, his score per weekend moves up to 22.3 points on average, easily his highest. His career total 67 points in Lusail is matched only by his tally from Spa-Francorchamps, though he’s raced there once more in his career so far. He’s competed in three sprints in Qatar and won every one of them, and though there’s no short race on the schedule this weekend, it shouldn’t prevent him from putting in a strong weekend. “My sprint record is going to be untouched, so that's good!” he joked. “It's always been a strong track for me in the past. Obviously last year could have been even better, but it's a track I've always enjoyed.” PIT TALK PODCAST: Max Verstappen wins an overtaking fest in Las Vegas and scores another victory in his rivalry with George Russell, and Marc Márquez clinches his eighth premier-class championship with a subdued grand prix performance in Portugal. | Listen to Pit Talk below > Piastri’s strength has always been his performance in fast corners, where his bravery and feel for the car on the edge of grip have set him apart. The Lusail International Circuit is all medium- and high-speed bends, with only one slow corner in the middle of the track. But part of the reason he’s been less effective this season is that the 2026 car uses fast corners to charge the battery, meaning they’re no longer limited by grip. Piastri can no longer make the difference. “It'll be interesting to see what it's like in these new cars because I think the high-speed section towards the end of the lap in the previous generation of cars was always right on the limit of being flat-out and was always an amazing section of track to drive,” he said. “We'll see if it's any different this year, but nice to be here and hopefully it can be a good weekend.” Even so, Piastri feels he’s made progress with the car through the year and in the second half of the season in particular. His progress at low-grip Las Vegas demonstrated how he’s minimised a traditional weakness. “I feel like I'm getting there,” he said. “The last five or six races have definitely been better — some have been good, some have been not so good still, but I think the general trend of things is definitely going in the right direction, so that's been the biggest lesson. “I'm looking forward to these last couple of races. Hopefully we can end the year on a bit of a better note and then obviously work very hard in the off-season to try and come back next year on the front foot and more on top of things.” FERRARI REMAINS COY ON TEAM ORDERS SITUATION Ferrari has a second chance to seal second place in the constructors championship, having squibbed its opportunity in Las Vegas. Its failure there was down almost completely to yet another on-track clash between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in an escalating rivalry for top status at the legendary team. Leclerc tipping Hamilton into a spin tipped team boss Fred Vasseur over the edge. He read the Monegasque the riot act before he could speak to the media, as the star driver’s decidedly downbeat post-race interviews suggested. Vasseur promised that discussions would continue through the week leading up to this weekend’s race after everyone had had time to process the events of Vegas. Speaking after a team meeting on Thursday in Qatar, Leclerc accepted that things had got out of hand between him and Hamilton. “It is unacceptable,” he said, echoing Vasseur’s words last weekend. “We cannot afford to clash between teammates, and I think that is very clear for everyone. “I think there's just tension around that we just need to dissipate and make sure that we look at more positive days in the future.” Though he said that “some level of tension is always there in top teams” when they field two evenly matched drivers, “it doesn't necessarily have to escalate, and that is why we need to find a solution and fix that”. Ferrari and its drivers have given nothing away about what consequences have stemmed from the Las Vegas clash, but it would appear that some kind of framework for internal racing rules has been settled. “I'm not going to disclose that,” Leclerc said when asked what solutions the team had come up with. “I'm not allowed to anyway, so I cannot go into the detail of that. “I would rather have these discussions internally.” Hamilton has been calling for months for Ferrari to come up with a set of rules that govern the way he and Leclerc race each other, with the first flashpoint being their first-lap clash at the Italian Grand Prix that ended with the Englishman losing positions after being guided off the road and into the stones. “You learn really through the hardest times, and these are definitely very, very challenging times for Fred and Charles and me,” he said, per Autosport. “But think these are the moments that you really learn and grow closer together through conversation and communicating and having those sit-downs." Hamilton revealed that he and Leclerc had dissected each of their clashes corner by corner in a bid to come up with a common understanding but added that he didn’t expect the team to implement any hard rules on how they battle each other. "You can never cover everything, because every scenario is different,” he said. "There's always going to be something new that you maybe haven't foreseen. You also have to use your instinct, and at the core you always have to have the team.” He added to Sky Sports: "We're still free to race. “Moving forwards, I think we're going to be fine. I'm just literally focused on racing hard and fair.” LECLERC DENIES RUMOURS OF NUMBER ONE STATUS Leclerc is signed up to Ferrari on a long-term contract, having been inside the Ferrari system for a decade, dating back to his days in GP3, and having long been central to its plans to return to title contention. Hamilton’s future is somewhat less certain, with his contract expiring next year — though the Briton is likely to seek an extension given his much-improved form with the change in regulations. There has been speculation online that their contrasting contractual status is playing a role in their on-track battles, with some spreading rumours that the Monegasque has a clause in his deal guaranteeing him number one driver status. “I normally never disclose what I have in my contract, but I think this one is an important one to speak about,” Leclerc said. “I absolutely have zero clause that says that in my contract. It's never something that I was interested in and never something that I personally wanted. So no, I don’t. “At the end of the day, [dealing with speculation] is part of our job. I think the only thing that I don't like seeing is people questioning my integrity to the team, my love for the team. “I think it's more the question mark of that that I have seen going around that hurts me more than anything else. “I think there's nothing clearer than the love I have for the team, and I will do absolutely everything in order to bring Ferrari back to the top.” The conflict at Ferrari is unusual for not being particularly personal. Unlike, for example, the rivalry between Max Verstappen and George Russell, there’s no real animosity between Leclerc and Hamilton, whose relationship off the track appears largely unaffected by their collisions on it. "We do enjoy racing together, and we do have a really good relationship,” Hamilton told Sky Sports. “It's obviously intense in the background; on the outside it seems a lot more intense than it does on the inside." Leclerc said the on-track incidents had not poisoned the team in the way some rivalries have done elsewhere. “We have a very good relationship outside the car with Lewis,” he said. “I wouldn't say the atmosphere is good, because obviously we are all disappointed for the situation we find ourselves in, but at the same time, we are all grown up and responsible of that, so we've got to find a solution. “We are the ones that need to find the solutions in order to make that better, so there's also a big willingness in trying to find a solution.” ANTONELLI ADMITS TO TITLE HANGOVER Andrea Kimi Antonelli has admitted sealing the world championship with four rounds to spare has affected his driving in the final part of the season. The Italian became the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history after finishing third in the Mexico City Grand Prix but hasn’t finished on the podium in the two races since then. He was leading the São Paulo Grand Prix when he spun off the road at the first corner while attempting to defend position ahead of Lando Norris and went on to finish the race fifth. He was contending for victory again in Las Vegas when a throttle error on the penultimate lap dropped him to fourth. It’s the first time this season Antonelli hasn’t appeared on the podium at consecutive weekends. Speaking ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix, with two rounds remaining, Antonelli admitted that adjusting to the pressure being completely off his performances had resulted in something of a championship hangover. "I've been enjoying but I've not been enjoying at the same time, because obviously the past races haven't gone well, I would say, despite having the pace," he said, per The Race. Both Piastri and Lando Norris made the most of the significant grunt in the Mercedes power unit on their MCL40s to make a significant indent on the field, amid a race-long sequence of yo-yo racing up and down the pack. We obviously got a little bit close at some points, but we were both very clear with what the goal was, which was to score as many points for the team as possible. "So we definitely didn’t race too hard, we raced each other very smart and ensured that we both stayed at the front." London [UK], November 25 (ANI): Indian ace cricketer Rishabh Pant swapped the cricket field for the Formula 1 simulator at McLaren’s facility, before turning the tables and introducing Australian driver Oscar Piastri to the finer points of batting in a delightful sporting crossover.Pant first got behind the wheel of McLaren’s racing simulator, with Piastri watching over as the Indian got a feel for the technicalities of driving an F1 car. It was then time for the Australian to step into Pant’s world.Taking Piastri to a level playing field, Pant picked up the role of coach, offering him underarm deliveries and helping him get his batting stance right. Piastri made a clean connection with the ball, much to Pant’s amusement, with the Indian joking that the McLaren driver could now join his team.The exchange had an added cricketing connection, as Piastri is a fan of the game and, more importantly, of former Australia captain Ricky Ponting. Getting a batting lesson from an Indian wicketkeeper-batter was therefore a rather enjoyable crossover for the Australian.In the case of Pant, the interaction has come amid a strong run of headlines on the cricket field. items.article_search_text: The McLaren boss highlights his drivers' ability to overcome the limitations of the MCL40 in Las Vegas. Despite the lack of top speed and the short gear ratios, both managed to come back and fight for the podium, exceeding the team's expectations. Andrea Stella has not spared praise towards his drivers after the Las Vegas Grand Prix and the McLaren [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/mclaren]boss, aware of the MCL40's limitations, has assured that the performance of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri on the urban circuit has been "one of their best races". The Briton finished second and the Australian third, a result that gains even more value taking into account the circumstances, since Piastri started seventeenth due to a power unit penalty and Norris came to fall outside the top 10 in the first laps. Stella broke down the three factors that complicated McLaren's race: "The car did not have enough inherent top speed, which has nothing to do with the power unit, because it is the same for all HPP cars. There was simply too much aerodynamic drag. The second factor is that we paid the price of having eighth gear too short, which is a problem, especially when you follow someone. The revs go up too much and the power drops too much. And the third factor is that the engineers discovered what was happening to Lando, why we were losing those positions, and what was working with Oscar, who was gaining positions. They worked harder than ever this season with the drivers to optimize the power unit deployment". F1 Las Vegas GP: What We Learned From Drivers' Complaints About Their Cars [https://deweb-519a7.b-cdn.net/post-images/e2b9eff3-40ad-4d68-b984-1dc656b5e918.jpeg] F1 Las Vegas GP: What We Learned From Drivers' Complaints About Their Cars Isack Hadjar, Kimi Antonelli, and their fellow drivers had car performance issues to report after the 2026 Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix. [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/f1-las-vegas-gp-what-we-learned-from-drivers-complaints-about-their-cars] The team director wanted to highlight the work of the engineers, who managed to compensate for the car's limitations with intelligent energy management: "Good news in terms of power unit exploitation, but other limitations, aerodynamic drag and gear ratios, were a problem today. However, the good work of Oscar and Lando and of the engineers compensated for these limitations". Stella's reflection went further and he acknowledged that the drivers performed beyond the car's possibilities: "In terms of drivers, let me say that I think for both, Oscar and Lando, this is one of their best races. Because the relationship between the result, what they were able to extract in terms of result, and what the team made available in terms of car potential, I think is one of the best for both. When for other cars it would have been fine to get out of the slipstream and complete an overtake, they realized: don't do it, because we are not going to be able to overtake. So there was a lot to process while you were practically at the limit keeping the car on track. Therefore, I would like to clearly praise that this is one of the best races for Oscar and Lando". Norris and McLaren’s Pending Debt: Testing the Upgrades in FP3 [https://deweb-519a7.b-cdn.net/post-images/d819a14d-f0e1-4431-9332-c1b9cee1428e.jpeg] Norris and McLaren’s Pending Debt: Testing the Upgrades in FP3 The Briton describes the third practice session as "fundamental" after an FP2 marked by rain that prevented evaluating the MCL40 updates. [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/norris-and-mclaren-s-pending-debt-testing-the-upgrades-in-fp3] For Piastri [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/f1-las-vegas-gp-predicting-the-start-of-sundays-race], the Las Vegas result is especially encouraging and the Australian has gone through a complicated season, but on the low-grip urban circuit and not very conducive to his style he demonstrated a confidence and a determination that had not been seen for months. Stella highlighted that recovery and the good sensations it leaves for the next races: "Already in Brazil I was quite happy with the improvement we saw in Oscar's pace. Here it was much clearer that, in addition to the power unit utilization and driving with little grip, Oscar drove with confidence and assertiveness. That means he is now in tune with the car. He can start to use his superpower, which is this race ability, this concentration. And that is very promising for the end of the season and for what we bring to the next". items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri offered a fiery response to warnings from his McLaren team to be careful around his team-mate Lando Norris during the Las Vegas GP; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live on Sky Sports this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday McLaren team principal Andrea Stella says he liked Oscar Piastri's fiery response to radio messages warning the Australian to "be careful" battling his team-mate Lando Norris during the Las Vegas Grand Prix. Piastri started from 17th on the grid after taking an engine penalty but drove impressively - during an extraordinary race that featured 352 overtakes - to join the battle at the front in latter stages, closing in on a leading train of cars that featured Norris. As Piastri chased George Russell for fourth with Norris just in front of the Mercedes, a radio exchange was played out on the television broadcast which featured him twice being told by his race engineer to "be careful" around his team-mate, to which he responded: "Stop telling me to ****ing be careful." F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts 📱 Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺 The McLaren pair ultimately benefitted from late errors by Russell and his Mercedes team-mate Antonelli to claim a double podium, with Norris second and Piastri third behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen. Asked about Piastri's radio exchange after the race, Stella said: "I actually liked it. I like it. That's the character that you expect from a racer. "It's not like the Michael Schumacher, the Fernando Alonso, the Kimi Raikkonen - that I worked with before - were any easier, and (they) were champions. "That's the character you want to see. And that's also what you have to do from the pit wall. You need to make sure that the driver has a clear objective in his head. "And you want to do it up until the point the driver makes you feel, 'I've got it. Don't go beyond.' That's exactly where you want to be from outside the cockpit. "So, actually, well done to the pit wall and well done to Oscar in relation to this situation. That's exactly where we want to position the interaction between the team and the driver, and what we have learnt through some of the experiences we've gone through." 'You have to modulate and adapt a driver's racing spirit' With Norris clearly outperforming Piastri this season, there have been relatively few challenges for McLaren in managing their drivers, which is in significant contrast to last season when Norris came out on top in a battle for the drivers' title that went down to the final race of the season. The only major flashpoint of this season came when an aggressive attempt to pass Piastri from Norris on the final lap of the Sprint in Singapore resulted in contact that cost both drivers points, leading to criticism from Stella and an apology from the Brit. Stella provided more detail on his approach to managing his drivers as he attempted to further explain why he liked Piastri's fierce radio response in Las Vegas. "I'll have to up a little bit of IP (intellectual property) here, in terms of how you manage drivers, but let me be clear, because we avoid this matter to create any noise," Stella said to gathered reporters. "If we go and we do a leisure go-karting together, our personalities will change slightly from the personality we have right now when we are enjoying sitting here. We will dig out the racing spirit, we will dig out something that is the reason why these guys do what they do, and all the sacrifices that they have gone through to be where they are. "And that's where you have to come and help them, come and help them modulate, adapt. We want to use it. That's why I said I really liked Oscar's answer. That's the racer I want to see. But at the same time, it's a team effort in modulating it. We want to use just the right quantity of it that doesn't take us too far. "And if you see Lando in Singapore, Lando certainly, you don't have to remind him of the team interest and that he's a team player. He's a phenomenal team player, yet his vision, his way of racing got a little too channelled, and in the final lap of the Sprint, he attacked Oscar in a way that led to a collision. "And he was incredibly apologetic. And, if anything, he said like, 'guys, just don't assume that we do all the processing, because we are so busy just racing, keeping the car on track, and this year's car absorbs our bandwidth. So, just help us. Take it to the point where we can tell you, 'ok, that's enough. I've got it.'' "And that's exactly the point where we want to take it. The same message was given to both drivers, because that's a common learning. This is nothing to do with Oscar, this is just to do with dealing with drivers." Stella's sympathy with all team bosses, not just Ferrari's Vasseur McLaren also benefitted in Las Vegas from Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc colliding when they were also in contention for the leading positions. Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for causing the collision which spun Hamilton, and ultimately led to Ferrari failing to maximise the solid race pace they produced. The incident was the latest in a series of clashes between the Ferrari drivers, with the previous one having cost the team a likely one-two in the Mexico City Grand Prix when Leclerc attempted to pass Hamilton for the lead on the opening lap. Asked whether he had sympathy for his Ferrari counterpart Frederic Vasseur, Stella said: "When it comes to commenting on other teams, that's something I would not want to do. I can only say that it's a very difficult subject. "Even last year, in which I would say we've been successful in managing two drivers in that sort of situation, fighting for their dream, which is the drivers' world championship, it's just been an incredible amount of work. "Work that sometimes, I say, we paid in the fact that 2026 was affected by the effort that we needed to put into 2025. "So, it's something that every team principal needs to deal with and it's probably one of the most difficult aspects to managing Formula 1, because it's the only one in which you can't simply say, 'let's go as a team.' "Because the drivers, they compete for themselves. So, definitely sympathy, but for team principals in general, not only for Fred." items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri's fired-up radio message in Las Vegas wasn't quite what it seemed — but was indicative of a driver finally finding form. Read more at foxsports.com.au. Oscar Piastri’s fired-up radio transmission in Las Vegas wasn’t quite what it seemed, but there was no doubting the Aussie’s improved form. Oscar Piastri had made 15 overtakes in less than 40 laps of the Las Vegas Grand Prix when the voice of his race engineer, Tom Stallard, filled his ears. “Oscar, you’re doing a great race, mate. Let’s be careful around our teammate. Please be careful around our teammate. I know you’re doing a great job.” The reply was swift and pointed. Fox Sports, available on Kayo Sports, is the only place to watch every practice, qualifying session and race in the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship™ LIVE in 4K | Get Kayo now > “Stop telling me to f***ing be careful.” Piastri must have been thinking that was the last thing he needed to hear in the middle of such a chaotic race. He’d made stunning progress up to that point. Starting from 17th on the grid, he was up to 12th on the first lap and rose to eighth — ahead of teammate Lando Norris — on lap 16, going great guns at a track that on paper shouldn’t have suited him well. The need to stack behind Norris at their sole stop behind the safety car dumped him back outside the points, but a great restart had him back into eighth immediately and with his sights set on a podium. With Norris’s car back filling his helmet visor, suddenly he was being told to be careful. The economy of words in his reply was typical of the Australian, but the fieriness wasn’t. Not since the deeply frustrating crash with backmarker Carlos Sainz in Hungary, scuppering his shot at beating Norris to victory, has he been so withering. There’s a temptation to read too much into team radio. Though on the one hand the messages are raw, unvarnished and therefore deeply authentic, they are on the other hand restricted by the medium. Drivers and engineers have to be short and sharp to get their points across as quickly and easily as possible. There was certainly no doubting Piastri’s desire from his message, and perhaps it was a sign of a greater willingness to fight for himself in a year he has marginalised himself through his own performances. But assuming this exchange reveals a loss of faith between team and driver would be a step too far. In fact it was by design — and targeted more at his teammate than at him. ‘I ACTUALLY LIKED IT’ McLaren gave both drivers the same message at the same part of the race. Norris’s reply was evidently less exciting and therefore didn’t make the television broadcast. Team principal Andrea Stella revealed after the race that the seemingly overbearing messages were prompted by Norris in the aftermath of him crashing into Piastri on the final lap of the sprint race in Singapore. Norris eventually took responsibility for causing the crash, apologising for what Stella described as a competitive tunnel vision getting the better of his team-first training. “His perspective, his way of driving, was a bit too focused on one thing,” Stella said, per Motorsport Total . “We want to utilise [that racing instinct], but at the same time, it’s a team task to manage it. We want to use exactly the right amount of it without going too far.” He said that Norris had told the team not to “assume [the drivers] make all these considerations ourselves”. “We’re so busy racing and keeping the car on the track,” he said Norris told him. “Just help us until we can say to you, ‘Okay, that’s enough; I understand’.” That’s exactly what played out on track in Las Vegas. Stella has been determined to foster a culture of openness at McLaren, including during race situations. That includes drivers saying what they think over team radio — better to leave everything on the table than to realise after the race that something had been lost in communication. “I actually liked it,” Stella said, per Motorsport , of Piastri’s sharp radio response in Las Vegas. “That’s the character that you expect from a racer. It’s not like Michael Schumacher, Fernando Alonso, Kimi Räikkönen, who I worked with before, were any easier. They were champions. That’s the character you want to see. “That’s also what you have to do from the pit wall. You need to make sure that the driver has a clear objective in his head, and you want to do it up until the point the driver makes you feel, ‘I got it. Don’t go beyond.’ “That’s exactly where you want to be from outside the cockpit. So actually: well done to the pit wall and well done to Oscar in relation to this situation. That’s exactly where we want to position the interaction between the team and the driver — and what we have learned through some of the experiences we have gone through.” THE FERRARI COUNTERPOINT It may come across as nannying, but Stella believes it’s a strategy that works for his team — perhaps as one of the elements of the so-called papaya rules that has survived into 2026. Critics would do well to consider whether McLaren’s approach delivered a better outcome than that of the three other frontrunning teams. For example: how’s Ferrari going? The Italian team has given the impression it is completely uninterested, unwilling or unable to lay down any kind of law to govern the way its drivers race each other. As a result, Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc have raced each other with increasing ferocity, both clearly aware that the leadership of the team is on the line — and, with it, perhaps first crack at a championship challenge next year. They’ve hit each other repeatedly this season and with escalating consequences. In Mexico their first-lap duel probably cost the team a victory, if not a one-two. In Las Vegas, Leclerc tipped Hamilton into a spin when they were both looking to score an unlikely podium at the team’s weakest track. Hamilton was clearly satisfied after the race that he had the moral high ground, and team boss Fred Vasseur later confirmed as much, having hauled in Leclerc immediately after the Monegasque got out of the car. Asked about the lack of driver management in the race, Hamilton made clear — as he has done all year — that it’s up to the team to decide what it wants. “That’s for Ferrari to decide,” he told Sky Sports. “I’ve done all I can; I’ve said everything and more. “It’s been difficult. All I can do is just show up and give it everything I can, and hopefully in the background they eventually figure it out.” Hamilton arrived from a Mercedes team that developed a strict structure following his and Nico Rosberg’s fractious title battles in 2014–16. Ferrari, though, has never really worked like that. Typically it’s had a clear lead driver by either performance or designation. Even when Carlos Sainz gave Leclerc a run for his money, they were such different drivers with such different performance profiles that they never really came into conflict. Hamilton and Leclerc, however, are in each other’s firing line. Of course Vasseur attempted to clear the air after their Mexico clash, sitting both of them down in Brazil to lay down the law. He and both drivers said afterwards that it was case closed — that they were all on the same page and understood how to race each other without compromising the team. They crashed again just one race after that meeting — despite having been warned, similar to the McLaren drivers, to take care while battling. "All the other teams, they were able to overtake each other 20 times during the race,” Vasseur said, per Autosport . “Honestly, you can't imagine the frustration for me” But his problem has become far bigger than just miscommunication. Ferrari hasn’t done the hard yards to reset the culture, and the problem has catastrophised since. “The pressure is certainly mounting, and now the situation is much worse than it was 18 months ago,” Vasseur told Italy’s Sky Sport. “Lately it’s become unmanageable between them. “I think there’s a misunderstanding on a human level between the two drivers, not between them and the team.” McLaren, on the other hand, had done the work to ensure its drivers never become unmanageable. “It’s a very difficult issue,” Stella said, per Motorsport Total . "Even last year, when I believe we were successful in managing two drivers in such a situation, it involved an incredible amount of work “That's probably one of the most difficult aspects of running a Formula 1 team, because it's the only area where you can't simply say: We'll do this together as a team." As Ferrari is realising, it takes more than just words from the drivers to be assured of the kind of teamwork it wants from both. WHAT NEXT FOR PIASTRI? McLaren has also had things relatively easy this year on the teammate front. Not only has it not been in contention for the big prizes, which always eases the pressure, but Piastri has spent most of the year well adrift of Norris. He hasn’t been a natural fit for this generation of car, and it’s taken him most of the season to adjust. He also hasn’t been helped by the McLaren being developed into an increasingly peaky corner, with the car having become more unpredictable to drive through the year. But after a barren run of results through the previous triple-header of races, Piastri executed perhaps the best performance of his season in Las Vegas. On a day many drivers struggled to retain positions gained through overtaking, Piastri made up a sensational number of places from what had looked like a pretty bleak 17th place on the grid ahead of a race in which McLaren expected to struggle for its lack of straight-line performance. Instead those circumstances allowed him to demonstrate how much progress he’s made understanding the 2026 car — and on a low-grip track of the sort his driving style has never been a particularly good match for. "I think Oscar drove with confidence and assertiveness, which means that he is now kind of in tune with the car," Stella said, per Motorsport . “He can start using his superpower, which is this racing ability, this focus. "That's very promising for the end of the season and what we carry into the next one." The next one is this weekend’s Qatar Grand Prix. The Losail International Circuit has been by far the most lucrative track of Piastri’s career to date. It’s one of only two circuits, along with Jeddah, where he’s never been beaten in a race by Norris. He also never finished off the podium in a grand prix, with a career-best average finishing position of 2.3. His average of 17 points per grand prix is the highest for any venue, and his career total 67 points across all race formats is matched only by Spa-Francorchamps, where he’s already competed this season. Of course all those numbers would have been higher had McLaren’s botched strategy at last year’s race not taken him out of the lead while on track for a comfortable victory. Like Norris, Piastri spent the majority of the race yo-yo racing in the tightly packed midfield, with overtaking moves happening every few corners. This included extended duels with his teammate, which had the McLaren pitwall hot under the collar, as the two papaya cars diced for what would eventually result in a double podium. I know you’re doing a great job.” Piastri's reply was both brutally short and to the point: “Stop telling me to f***ing be careful.” The two McLarens were in close quarters during the Las Vegas GP Oscar Piastri defends radio rebuke After the race, Piastri defended his expletive rebuke, hinting that the drivers knew what was at stake, and they had never planned on racing over the limit of acceptability. “Yeah, we know what we’re doing. Oscar Piastri completed the podium for McLaren, 1.529 seconds behind the winner. Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes finished fourth, followed by Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto, according to the official Formula 1 race report. Verstappen started from pole position after Antonelli, the fastest driver in qualifying, took a five-place grid penalty for a power unit change. George Russell of Mercedes pressed the Dutchman for much of the 50 laps, and the two traded the lead several times. Russell locked up on lap 48 and dropped to ninth, while Antonelli appeared to suffer a problem and slipped behind both McLarens. "It was just a crazy amount of fighting," Verstappen said, adding that the slipstream on the long straights made it almost impossible to pull clear. It was his third victory at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. A Safety Car was deployed mid-race after Sergio Perez of Cadillac collided with Haas driver Rafael Camara. Perez retired from the race. Red Bull's Isack Hadjar ran third after the restart but lost his front wing and fell back. He finished 14th on the road, and a 10-second post-race penalty moved him down to 15th. Ferrari had a difficult night. Lewis Hamilton took a 10-second penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage while fighting Norris, and later made contact with his team-mate Charles Leclerc. Leclerc received a 10-second penalty of his own. Hamilton finished seventh and Leclerc tenth, with Carlos Sainz eighth for Williams in his 250th Grand Prix. RaceFans' points table shows Antonelli on 402 points, Verstappen on 304 and Hamilton on 267 after 21 of 23 rounds. Oscar Piastri enjoyed a Las Vegas overtaking masterclass, with the Australian claiming an unexpected Formula 1 podium from the back of the grid. In a difficult season for the McLaren driver, Piastri headed to the 'gambling capital of the world' to test his luck in F1. Ahead of the weekend, chances looked grim, as the Australian was hit with a ten-place grid penalty, in a season where the MCL40 has struggled for pace. But despite starting 17th in Vegas, Piastri capitalised on the chaos and close racing through the field, slowly moving his McLaren into the top spots, challenging his team-mate Lando Norris and the Mercedes duo in particular. Reflecting on the race, the 25-year-old highlighted that it was a strategic race for the ages. The Safety Car and Mercedes' mistakes, in particular, played into McLaren's hands for a double podium. "Yeah, it was crazy," Piastri concluded. "I think, as Lando kind of said, it was a lot about playing your cards at the right time." "I think from where I was, I think we were very quick in the corners, so then you could stay very close in the slipstream, which was good." "But yeah, the timing of the safety car was a bit unfortunate because we had to do a double stack in the pit stop, so I kind of went back again and had to fight my way back." Piastri understood from very early in the race that the race was going to be chaotic. Thus, opening many opportunities for himself to get to the front of the pack. Crucially, the McLaren driver played his cards right and was very happy with an unexpected second-place finish. "But no, from that far back, I think I kind of worked out pretty early on that it was going to be a pretty chaotic race. And that there were going to be a lot of opportunities throughout the whole thing. Even from where we were." "So, I'm very happy that we made the right decisions at the right time and were able to end up on the podium." https://twitter.com/F1/status/2124408791643082897?a=T4luaNAdsRLDoYshzSk&s=20 Oscar Piastri explains MCL40 handling issues despite Las Vegas podium Whilst the Australian secured just his third podium of the season, it hasn't eradicated the issues he has faced with this year's challenger. Throughout the season, Piastri has struggled to extract the same pace as his team-mate Norris, ulimately having a more difficult time adjusting to the sweeping 2026 regulations. When asked if this was the most comfortable he's been all season, Piastri explained the rollercoaster his season has been with the MCL40. "No, I don't think so," he said. "The last few races have been up and down. "I think the ups have been back at the level that they should be. And the downs obviously are not where they should be." However, there was still a higher level of comfort at times throughout the weekend than what Piastri has grown accustomed to in previous races. Ultimately, the McLaren driver pointed to the team's development for next season, where they will hopefully return to form. "But yeah, I was a bit more comfortable this weekend, not necessarily all the time. But again, I think we're still working on it." "Some things hopefully will be better next year. We'll see. McLaren strengthened its challenge for the Formula 1 Constructors' Championship with a double podium at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, where Oscar Piastri recovered from 17th on the grid to finish third. The Australian described the result as an important boost for the team after an eventful 50-lap race on the Las Vegas street circuit.According to Formula 1, Piastri started 17th after receiving a 10-place grid penalty for changing power unit components ahead of the weekend. He worked his way through the field before challenging teammate Lando Norris for the final podium position.Both McLaren drivers overtook Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes on the final lap, securing the team's second double podium of the season. The result also reduced McLaren's deficit to Red Bull to nine points in the Constructors' Championship, despite Max Verstappen taking the race victory.Piastri highlighted the team's recovery during the race and the importance of collecting points in the championship battle."It was a lot of fun. It was pretty entertaining, that’s for sure. It was just a crazy race," said Piastri.The Australian explained that his progress during the opening laps was interrupted by the timing of the Safety Car. He also lost ground after stopping behind Norris during the pit sequence before fighting his way back toward the front."I made really good progress in the first few laps, and then a bit unfortunate with the timing of the Safety Car so I kind of dropped back halfway again [after stacking behind Norris in the pits]. Made our way towards the front, which was great, and I think also for the team this was exactly the kind of result we needed for the Constructors’ Championship. Very happy with the day’s work."The Las Vegas result marked Piastri's third podium of the season. His previous appearance on the podium came at the Miami Grand Prix in May, while Norris had secured three victories during the campaign.Despite welcoming his latest podium, Piastri remained cautious about what the performance meant for his overall pace. He noted that the unusual characteristics of the Las Vegas race made it difficult to draw firm conclusions about McLaren's progress."It’s hard to say. Definitely I think the pace in general was pretty strong so I was happy with things, but that was such a particular race," said Piastri.He also pointed to the differences expected at the upcoming events, emphasizing that the team would need to maintain its performance across different racing conditions."The next two weeks are not going to look like that, that’s for sure. I think the pace was good so we’ll just try and keep it rolling for the next two weeks."

items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri questions McLaren's straight-line speed deficit against other Mercedes-powered cars after a disappointing Las Vegas qualifying session. McLaren's straight-line speed disadvantage has raised fresh concerns after Oscar Piastri questioned why the team trails other Mercedes-powered competitors at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. The Australian driver highlighted an unexpected performance gap during qualifying, despite McLaren anticipating difficulties at the high-speed circuit.Piastri secured seventh place in final qualifying, while teammate Lando Norris finished fifth. However, Piastri faces a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding Formula 1's seasonal allowance of four internal combustion engines after installing his fifth unit.According to Motorsport.com, Piastri also received an upgraded turbocharger specification developed by Mercedes through the FIA's Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) framework.Piastri acknowledged that his qualifying performance had been inconsistent, particularly during the decisive third session."After Q2, I was pretty happy with how it went," Piastri said.He explained that securing an effective slipstream was particularly important at the Las Vegas circuit, where small differences in energy deployment could significantly affect straight-line performance."And then Q3 was just a bit messy for a few reasons. Trying to get the right slipstream is… you might as well not even go out if you don't get that right," Piastri said.He also identified differences in how cars manage energy before the opening corner as another factor affecting their speed later in the lap."Even opening the lap here, I think there's a bit of a difference between cars, how much energy they use to turn one and if that's half a second, that can be the difference of three or four tenths down the straight later in the lap," Piastri said.McLaren's performance difficulties are linked partly to aerodynamic limitations and its technical decisions. The team selected lower gear ratios and the shortest permissible wheelbase to reduce weight, choices that have restricted some opportunities to improve aerodynamic performance.The team also introduced a revised floor for Las Vegas, but only one specification was ready in time for the event. Norris received the updated component, although his Q3 performance was affected when a plastic bag became trapped around one of its floor fences.Piastri said the difference between McLaren and other Mercedes-powered cars was particularly difficult to explain."It's difficult to know and it caught us by surprise, to be honest. I don't think we expected it to be such a big problem. At Monza we were okay and the strange part for us is it's mostly compared with the other Mercedes-powered cars," Piastri said.He suggested that differences in aerodynamic downforce configurations could be contributing to the performance gap, although he acknowledged that the team still needed to understand the underlying problem."So, maybe a lot of people took downforce off and we didn't take enough off, but it seems like a pretty massive step that we were missing in practice. I don't know if it's still the same now, but definitely we seem, for one reason or another, to be pretty slow on the straights," Piastri said.Telemetry data from the fastest Q3 laps showed Piastri losing as much as 10 kilometers per hour to Alpine drivers Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly on the main straight along the Las Vegas Strip. Piastri compensated by braking later and maintaining throttle deeper into several corners.McLaren team principal Andrea Stella acknowledged that the circuit exposed weaknesses in the car's overall performance, particularly when aerodynamic drag, engine characteristics and slipstream effects combined."Definitely, we had some concern in terms of how suitable the demand of this circuit will be for our car," Stella said.Stella explained that the team's existing gear ratios and aerodynamic characteristics affected its ability to maximize performance at high speeds. He emphasized that McLaren needed to evaluate several interacting factors rather than focusing exclusively on maximum speed."For reasons that we have talked about before, developing speed at very high speed. Because this is not only the top speed, it is also the top speed that combines with the towing that everyone tries to see. So, you go in operating regimes of the engine that with our [gear] ratios are not ideal.We know that the drag from an aerodynamic point of view is not a point of strength. But we discussed in the debrief that we need to look holistically at all the conditions that influence the top speed," Stella said.Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli demonstrated the potential advantage of slipstreaming by recording the fastest time while running closely behind Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad. The Las Vegas circuit's slippery slow corners and cold November conditions made the aerodynamic effects of following another car less damaging to cornering performance.

items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri defended McLaren's racing approach after finishing third in Las Vegas, insisting he and Lando Norris understood how to compete safely. McLaren secured a valuable double podium at the Las Vegas Grand Prix after Oscar Piastri recovered from 17th on the grid to finish third behind Max Verstappen and Lando Norris. The Australian driver also dismissed suggestions that he and Norris needed additional instructions from the team while competing against each other during the closing stages of the race.According to Motorsport.com, Piastri started with a 10-place grid penalty following an engine change. His third-place finish marked his first podium since the Miami Grand Prix in May, while Norris secured second behind race winner Verstappen.The two McLaren drivers engaged in a late-race battle, with Norris eventually overtaking his teammate. The team's management had reminded both drivers to exercise caution, but Piastri maintained that they already understood their responsibilities on track.Responding to questions from Sky Sports about the team's instructions, Piastri defended their racing judgment."Yeah, we know what we're doing. We don't need to be told," said Piastri.He emphasized that maximizing the team's championship points remained their priority despite the close competition. Both drivers managed the situation without allowing their fight to compromise McLaren's result."For the team, that was a great result. We obviously got a little bit close at some points, but we were both very clear with what the goal was, which was to score as many points for the team as possible. So we definitely didn't race too hard. We raced each other very smart," Piastri said.Piastri also described the Las Vegas race as "bizarre" because of the unusual effects of aerodynamic slipstreaming, which made it difficult for drivers to establish a comfortable gap. He said McLaren generally had competitive pace but lacked some speed on the straights while performing better through corners."Obviously a massive pack, the slipstream being so important. Our pace generally was pretty good. We're obviously lacking a bit on the straights, but we're making up for it in the corners.It was just a bit odd in terms of the overtaking and where you would overtake. It wasn't normal. There was a bit of strategy involved with the buttons used, and where to use your energy, where to save it and stuff like that," Piastri said.Earlier in the Las Vegas weekend, both McLaren drivers had faced challenging weather conditions during Friday practice. According to GrandPrix.com, Piastri finished fifth in FP2 with a time of 1:48.453, while Norris placed seventh in 1:48.837.Piastri explained that skipping FP1 was a deliberate decision because heavy rain limited the value of running. FP2 provided an opportunity to gather information about the new internal combustion engine and turbocharger following his engine-related grid penalty."Overall, a positive session in FP2 after we chose not to run in FP1. With the rain in FP1, it didn't make much sense to go out as we weren't going to learn much, the conditions were bad, and we don't anticipate the rest of the weekend being the same. It was useful to get running in FP2 with the new Internal Combustion Engine and turbo so that we could learn as much as we could.It was an interesting and challenging session, with some good learnings on tyre warm-up. The initial few laps on the Inters were tricky but the car felt much more manageable as the conditions improved towards the end of the session, as a drier line started to appear. Looking ahead to tomorrow, while I have a 10-place grid penalty, it doesn't change our approach to the weekend.We will do what we can to maximise everything ahead of Qualifying and get ourselves up as high up as we can," Piastri said.Norris also highlighted the difficulties created by the wet surface and low temperatures. He said the team needed additional preparation before qualifying, particularly to evaluate new components and understand the car's behavior in dry conditions."It's good to be back on track here in Las Vegas, it's always an interesting place to drive an F1 car. This is a very low-grip, low-temperature circuit, and that's only been made more so by the rain today. In FP1, the level of rain meant there wasn't much value in going out, particularly when we expect it to be dry the rest of the weekend, but it was good to get some laps in during FP2, even if the conditions were still damp.We've got some important work to do tomorrow, particularly on testing some new bits and getting ready for Quali in dry conditions, so FP3 will be important. We'll do the best we can with the data we've gathered today and make sure we're ready to go tomorrow afternoon," Norris said.McLaren Senior Director of Racing Randy Singh explained that the weather also affected the team's technical development program. The engineers decided against installing a new floor because wet conditions and sensor limitations prevented them from collecting sufficiently reliable data."The conditions made it difficult to evaluate the car properly. In the wet, we had to tape up some of the sensors, which meant we could not always get the evidence we wanted, so we decided not to fit the new floor because of the risk and because we did not think we would learn much from it in these conditions. We hope to run it tomorrow and assess it more effectively.The rain and standing water made the track challenging, particularly with the walls so close, although the tyres held up well and we were able to do some useful work on the Intermediates as the rain eased. With both sessions wet, there is a lot to get through tomorrow, including preparation for Qualifying, and the programme will be compressed. It is clearly impossible to draw conclusions about our pace or likely positions: as usual, we can expect that the top four teams will be very close to each other, and the limited running of today makes it even more difficult to predict what there will be on the starting grid," Singh said.In the championship standings, Norris occupies fifth place with 264 points, level with George Russell in fourth according to Motorsport.com. Piastri sits seventh with 167 points, leaving McLaren with two drivers positioned inside the top seven as the season approaches its final two rounds.Mercedes also reported mixed findings from the rain-affected practice sessions. Russell topped FP2 with 1:47.272, although the team acknowledged that his fastest lap came when the circuit was at its driest. Kimi Antonelli finished eighth with 1:49.043."It's always nice to finish top of the times, but we know that doesn't tell the full story today. The conditions were changing throughout, and we got our lap in when the track was at its driest, while others looked very quick too. We weren't as competitive in the wet as we were last weekend, so there are a few things for us to understand overnight.Tomorrow will be busy if it stays dry and we'll want to maximise the running ahead of qualifying, particularly to learn about the tyres and any potential graining in these cold conditions. I'm feeling good at the moment though. We've been on the front row at the last two races, the performances have been strong, and this is a circuit I really enjoy.Hopefully we can build on that and have another good weekend," Russell said.Antonelli described the limited track time as an obstacle to establishing a consistent driving rhythm. He also identified intermediate-tyre performance as an area requiring further investigation."It was a strange day with the weather meaning we didn't get any real running in FP1 and no real representative running in FP2. It wasn't the easiest day therefore to build a rhythm. We still managed to learn a few things though and we have some things to look through overnight.We weren't as competitive as we would have liked on the Intermediate tyre so that will be useful to explore, even if it isn't learning that we will need for the rest of the weekend here in Las Vegas. Tomorrow should be a very different day if it stays dry, and FP3 will therefore be important. We'll need to maximise the running, get comfortable with the car in those conditions and understand the tyres, particularly with the limited information everyone has from today.I'm feeling positive though. The car has been performing well recently and hopefully we can have a productive final practice and put ourselves in a good position for qualifying," Antonelli said.
